body.cap: The image above is not a robot movie poster. M.AX stands for Manufacturing AX, or Manufacturing AI Transformation, and is a policy term used within the next-generation industrial strategy framework promoted by Korea’s Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy. It is not a simple brand name, but a strategic concept that signifies a fundamental, AI-based transformation of the entire manufacturing industry and a key keyword symbolizing Korea’s national industrial transition. | Photo by AVING News

body.x: The word most frequently mentioned on the CES 2026 keynote stage was “AI,” but the real theme running through the exhibition floor was far clearer. AI is no longer an algorithm confined to a screen. It has become something that moves. At the center of this shift stood robots, particularly humanoids.

Global semiconductor and computing companies, including AMD, pointed to “Physical AI” as the next destination of AI computation. In contrast, global manufacturing giants such as Hyundai Motor Group and LG positioned robots not as future concepts but as industrial assets ready for immediate deployment. CES 2026 clearly showed that the event has fully transformed from an exhibition of TVs and home appliances into a competitive arena for robots.

body.cap: The Humanoid M.AX Alliance joint pavilion at CES 2026, drawing constant crowds of global robot companies, buyers, and media. | Photo by AVING News
Neuromeka’s humanoid robot was unveiled at CES 2026, emphasizing precision control and industrial applicability. | Photo by AVING News

body.x: Amid these changes, one of the spaces that stood out most strongly was the Humanoid M.AX Alliance joint pavilion at CES 2026. Rather than listing individual company technologies, the Humanoid M.AX (Manufacturing AX) Alliance Pavilion presented the structure and strategy of Korea’s humanoid industry as a whole, condensed into a single space. On-site, remarks such as “a must-see pavilion at CES 2026” and “one of the most threatening robot booths” naturally circulated.

The M.AX Alliance Pavilion is not an exhibition led by a single organization. The Ministry of Trade, Industry, and Energy sets the policy direction, while the Korea Institute for Advancement of Technology acts as the overall secretariat overseeing the entire M.AX Alliance. The practical operation of the humanoid division is carried out through cooperation between the Korea Institute for Robot Industry Advancement and the Korea Association of Robot Industry. The structure itself, where policy, public institutions, and industry operate as a single flow rather than in separation, delivers the core message of this joint pavilion.

body.cap: Global engineers and representatives of Korean robot companies participating in the M.AX Alliance examine humanoid robot hand technologies together. | Photo by AVING News
Global visitors at the Humanoid M.AX Alliance Pavilion closely examine robot hand technologies and show strong interest in Korea’s collective humanoid strategy. | Photo by AVING News

body.x: The exhibition concept was also clear. The M.AX Alliance Pavilion chose a field-oriented demonstration over a simple technology display. Instead of placing a single robot on display, multiple types of robots were demonstrated in real manufacturing environments, intuitively showing where and how they are used.

This structure goes beyond passive viewing and allows demand companies, component suppliers, and large enterprise delegations to begin business discussions on the spot. The strategic decision to locate the pavilion in the Enterprise AI Zone rather than Eureka Park also signals an intention to position humanoids not as startup technologies, but as solutions ready for immediate industrial deployment.

The response on site was intense. Crowds filled the pavilion throughout the exhibition period, and VIP inbound tour schedules closed early for two consecutive days. Visitors included members of the National Assembly, local governments, public institutions, and representatives from major corporations such as Doosan, Samsung SDS, LG, and KT. Meetings focused not on simple observation but on exploring concrete collaboration opportunities. Comments like “this is the first time I’ve seen this many people gathered at a hardware robot booth” emerged on site. Within the industry, some even described the M.AX Alliance Pavilion as “worthy of a CES 2026 Top 10.”

body.cap: From left, Byoung-Tak Zhang, professor at Seoul National University and inaugural chair of the Humanoid M.AX Alliance, Jae-kwon Han, CEO of AEIROBOT, and Jang-beom Park, president of KBS, tour the M.AX Alliance Pavilion at CES 2026. | Photo by AVING News

body.x: Professor Byoung-Tak Zhang of Seoul National University defined the Humanoid M.AX Alliance as “a collective strategic choice made by Korea to leap toward becoming a global humanoid powerhouse, and a declaration of a national robotics strategy.” Since its launch in April last year with around 40 companies and universities, the alliance has expanded rapidly to include more than 250 partners, spanning AI companies, robot manufacturers, core component suppliers, universities, research institutes, and even demand-side companies that actually use robots. Professor Zhang explained that this pace of growth itself indicates both the sense of crisis and the rising expectations surrounding the humanoid industry.

He described humanoid robots as the core battleground of the Physical AI era that follows generative AI and as the final stage in which AI technology takes physical form in industrial settings. With explosive growth expected in the global humanoid market over the next decade, he noted that Korea would struggle to surpass the U.S.–China duopoly if it remained confined to competition among individual companies.

“The biggest differentiator is that those who create the technology and those who actually use it are bound together in a single alliance,” he said, emphasizing that a structure where research, development, demonstration, and demand remain connected defines the essence of Korea’s humanoid strategy. He added, “The Humanoid M.AX Alliance is not a simple consultative body, but a platform where the public and private sectors jointly design both the direction and the speed of the humanoid industry,” making clear the goal of securing leadership not only in technology competition but also in global standards and ecosystem competition.

body.cap: Gi-won Kang, president of the Korea Institute of Robotics & Technology Convergence, gives an interview at CES 2026 with the Humanoid M.AX Alliance Pavilion in the background. | Photo by AVING News

body.x: Clear perspectives also emerged regarding the global competitive landscape. Gi-won Kang, president of the Korea Institute of Robotics & Technology Convergence, described the joint pavilion as “a rare scene where a national team has formed in the robotics field.” While the United States drives its robot industry through Big Tech–centered AI model competition, China expands through state-led scale, and Korea chooses to bundle its limited resources through an alliance. He explained that sharing scattered technologies and jointly developing what is needed represents a realistic strategic bet for Korea’s humanoid industry.

President Kang especially highlighted Korea’s data competitiveness. Vast manufacturing process data accumulated on factory floors, world-class ICT and telecommunications infrastructure, and high-complexity surgical data gathered in medical settings stand as core assets in the Physical AI era.

An overall view of the Humanoid M.AX Alliance Pavilion, where the entire value chain, from core drive components and precision reducers to sensors, robot hands, control technologies, and complete humanoid robots, appears unified within a single alliance framework. | Photo by AVING News

Complete humanoid robots displayed at the Humanoid M.AX Alliance Pavilion, symbolically demonstrating Korea’s humanoid strategy implemented as a unified alliance from components to finished systems through live operation demonstrations. | Photo by AVING News

body.x: “The age of ideas is over. Now it is a war of collective strategies that move robots.”

Innovation is no longer a matter of ideas, but of collective execution. From the exhibition's opening day, keynotes and primary conference stages consistently placed robots at the forefront. The transition from generative AI to the Physical AI era was announced, and corporations from each country presented their robot strategies and application scenarios in turn. CES 2026 no longer serves as a place to forecast technology trends, but resembles an opening ceremony for a full-scale robot war to determine who can first deploy robots into real industrial battlefields.

Within this fierce competitive landscape, the Humanoid M.AX Alliance Pavilion attracted robot companies and global brand representatives from neighboring countries, who repeatedly asked, “Why is Korea so tightly unified?” and “How does this structure actually work?”

body.cap: Visitors listen to explanations of humanoid technologies and record videos in real time at the M.AX Alliance Pavilion. | Photo by AVING News
Visitors watch a live demonstration of AEIROBOT’s humanoid robot ALICE at the company’s booth within the M.AX Alliance Pavilion. | Photo by AVING News

body.x: This was not a demonstration of a single company’s technology, but a rare case showing how an entire nation designs and executes its robot industry. In the middle of the CES 2026 exhibition hall, now transformed into a battlefield for robots, the M.AX Alliance Pavilion naturally became a reference point.

At a time when global corporations take the stage with robots, Korea responds not as a single company but as a national team through the M.AX Alliance. This alliance, which binds research, development, manufacturing, components, and real demand into a single structure, goes beyond an exhibition strategy and serves as both Korea’s chosen survival strategy in the global robot industry and a declaration of challenge.
If CES 2026 asked, “Who can build robots?” the answer offered by the M.AX Alliance is clear. “We are already moving together.”
